extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and practicing online journalists, newsroom editors, and journalism students
extracted.subtask_description: An instructional/educational overview of the core characteristics, practical standards, and implementation choices that define high-quality online journalism, centered on immediacy, multimedia, interactivity, and hypertextuality. Useful for journalists and newsrooms designing online coverage and workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediacy (always-on news cycle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Online journalism's most striking feature is its speed: the internet dismantles fixed deadlines and makes the 'deadline' continuous. Stories are published immediately as events break and then updated over time as new information arrives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat online stories as a 'living document' — start with brief alerts or headlines and add details, quotes, and context as situations develop; use timestamped updates so readers can see how a story evolved. Be aware that the constant update cycle changes newsroom workflows compared with traditional scheduled publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification and transparent correction
rubrics_metrics.description: Because speed can cause initial reports to rely on incomplete or unverified information, verification sometimes happens after publication; transparent correction and updating are defining practices in the digital environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish corrections and updates openly (with timestamps and notes) rather than silently editing; recognise that while transparent correction is a strength, frequent post-publication corrections can raise public trust questions. Balance the need to publish quickly with verification practices to minimise avoidable errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real-time reporting benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Real-time reporting provides immediate, practical value — during disasters, elections, or market moves — delivering life-saving information, timely analysis, and a sense of global connectedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise speed for information that has urgent public value (evacuation routes, election results, market alerts). Use real-time updates to serve audiences who need immediate, actionable information, but document sources and verification steps as you update.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multimedia integration (multimediality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Online journalism routinely combines text, images, audio, video, infographics, data visualisations, interactive maps, and animations into a single story package.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design story packages that purposefully use multiple media types to enhance understanding and immersion. Multimedia is now a routine part of everyday news articles, not only special features; ensure technical and editorial workflows support multi-format production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match media format to story purpose (avoid multimedia for its own sake)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each media format serves specific purposes (text = narrative backbone; photos = visual evidence/emotion; video = showing events; audio = voices/ambient sound; infographics = explain complex stats; interactive maps = geographic data).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply editorial judgment to choose which elements genuinely enhance the audience’s understanding. Not every story needs video or an interactive chart — include multimedia only when it serves the story, not as an add-on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalists' expanded skill set
rubrics_metrics.description: The modern online journalist needs skills beyond strong writing — photography, basic video editing, audio recording, data handling, and editorial judgment about format choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in cross-training or specialist roles within the newsroom to ensure journalists can produce and integrate multimedia well. Assess capacity realistically: if a newsroom lacks resources for certain formats, avoid promising features you cannot sustain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interactivity (audience participation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Online news turns consumption into a two-way exchange: audiences can engage directly with content and journalists through comments, polls, social sharing, and other interactive features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use interactivity to create involvement and community, and to close feedback loops that help reporters identify resonant stories or missing angles. Consider how interactive features change editorial responsibilities and audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of interactivity: navigational, functional, adaptive
rubrics_metrics.description: Interactivity manifests as navigational interactivity (reader control of how they move through content), functional interactivity (comments, polls, quizzes, share buttons), and adaptive interactivity (personalisation and recommendation based on behaviour).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement navigational features (filters, topic jumps) to empower readers; use functional tools to solicit and surface audience input; deploy adaptive personalisation carefully to increase relevance without creating filter bubbles or undermining editorial diversity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation and management of interactive spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Interactive features can invite trolling, misinformation, and personal attacks; managing these spaces requires moderation resources and policy choices (e.g., disabling comments, requiring verification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan moderation strategies and resource allocation before enabling open interaction. Experiment with models (open comments, moderated threads, verified identities) to balance open engagement with civil discourse and factual reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypertextuality (use of hyperlinks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypertextuality — using hyperlinks to connect content — turns a single article into a gateway to a wider information ecosystem, linking to background documents, related stories, source materials, data sets, and external websites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use links to provide transparency, let readers verify sources, and deepen understanding. Recognise hypertextuality as a structural feature that changes how readers navigate and consume journalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal vs external linking strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal hyperlinks connect to content within the same site (keeping readers on the publisher’s domain and building depth); external hyperlinks point to outside sources (government reports, research papers, competing coverage) and enhance transparency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance internal links that improve on-site engagement with external links that allow readers to verify sources. Avoid the anti-pattern of underutilising external links purely for traffic retention, which can reduce transparency and reader trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic hyperlinking to avoid reader fragmentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyperlinks empower the reader to navigate non-linearly, but excessive or poorly placed links can fragment attention and distract from the core narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use hyperlinks strategically to add depth without pulling readers away before they absorb the core story. Structure in-article links and gating/contextual cues so readers can choose deep dives without losing the main thread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrated application of the four characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Immediacy, multimedia, interactivity, and hypertextuality function as an interconnected system rather than isolated features; combined, they can produce reporting that is richer, faster, deeper, and more participatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate workflows so speed, formats, audience engagement, and linking reinforce each other (example: breaking earthquake coverage that combines timely alerts, maps, videos, user reports, and source links). Design editorial processes that combine these elements coherently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource and ethical challenges (accuracy, capacity, misinformation, overload)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each core characteristic brings challenges: immediacy can compromise accuracy; multimedia requires resources/skills; interactivity can spread misinformation or abuse; hypertextuality can fragment attention; overall, there's a risk of information overload.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about trade-offs and set newsroom standards to mitigate harms: allocate verification resources for fast publishing, invest in multimedia capacity proportionate to demand, enforce moderation policies, design linking and UX to reduce overload, and prioritise using tools judiciously to serve the story and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of judicious use of tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Good online journalism is not about using every available tool — it is about using them judiciously to serve the story and the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt editorial criteria that evaluate whether a given tool (video, interactive map, live update, comments) materially improves reader understanding or public value. Avoid feature bloat driven by novelty, traffic goals, or production showmanship.
